theme_and_runs.why: Unmistakably a mini-game with goal, par, win and lose states and short sessions; I played it end to end with zero console output, all 25 static checks pass, all six reference solutions verifiably win inside the shipped rules (L2 solved at gen 20 in-browser), and every edge case I could invent is refused visibly and gracefully - empty garden warned, overplanting, planting mid-grow, stepping past the limit, reset restoring the planting, and no timer left running after leaving the screen.

originality.why: Not on the clone list and the framing is genuinely fresh - Life as one-shot puzzle golf where you plant, press Grow and never touch the garden again, with levels designed backwards from a verified seed so the par and the hint fall out of the construction; but Conway's Life is the single most familiar automaton to a developer jury, so the novelty sits in the wrapper rather than the simulation.

ux_design.why: Coherent soil-and-chlorophyll palette, real buttons with focus rings, aria-live status, per-cell labels, lit buds distinguished by shape as well as colour, reduced motion honoured, animated CSS rule cards instead of a text wall, and a clean fit from 320px to 1440px with 44px targets and pointer drag; held back by a very dim board where empty cells and unplanted seeds barely separate from the background on a phone, a win overlay that hides the pattern you just built, large dead space on desktop, no focus trap behind aria-modal, and an H hint key that is bound but unlisted.

prompt_quality.why: Specifies behaviour not code and anticipates the real unsupervised-agent failure modes - file:// module blocking, orphaned timers, localStorage throwing, foreign stored data - and its standout move, 'design every level backwards from a verified seed and solve it in the shipped build', turns an uncheckable requirement into a procedure that also yields the generation limit and the hint data; it loses a point on economy, since section 8's checklist restates sections 5 and 7 almost line for line and several constraints are stated three times.

reproducibility.why: Everything load-bearing is pinned - B3/S23 on a bounded grid computed into a new buffer, four generations per second, six named levels in a stated teaching order, every screen and keybinding enumerated, hint cap and penalty, scoring and storage semantics - so a rerun would clearly land the same game; the only open items are the exact boards, and the backwards-design procedure is what makes leaving them open safe, though it remains the step a rushed rerun is most likely to shortcut.

key_features_a_rerun_must_reproduce: Plant at most N seeds on a bounded grid, then press Grow and watch B3/S23 run without further input - winning the instant one generation lights every bud at once
Six levels designed backwards from a verified seed pattern, each provably solvable, unlocking in order
Reset returning to your planting with seeds intact in one click, plus a losing report that names the best moment ('3 of 4 buds, at generation 11')
Hint revealing one reference-solution cell at a capped, scored penalty, never one already planted
Full pointer, touch-drag and keyboard control with a visible cursor, and a status bar showing level, seeds left, generation of limit and buds lit
Survives localStorage being unavailable, falling back to in-memory progress with no console errors
biggest_weakness: The screen the player actually lives on is the weakest-looking one: the garden reads as a near-black grid where empty cells barely separate from the background and an unplanted seed is a dim green dot that is genuinely hard to spot at 375px, which undersells a mechanic whose whole appeal is watching a pattern you predicted come to life. Compounding it, the win overlay covers the board, so you never see the bloom you just engineered.
single_highest_leverage_fix: Lift the board's contrast - a lighter empty-cell fill against the soil and a bigger, brighter unplanted-seed token - and shrink or offset the win card so the solved garden stays visible behind it; it is a few lines of CSS and it makes the core loop legible at a glance on a phone.
